## Numbers 2 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

This chapter provides the divinely commanded arrangement of the twelve tribes around the tabernacle, both for encampment and for marching. The tabernacle sits at the centre, surrounded by the Levites, with the twelve tribes arranged in four groups of three on each cardinal side: Judah on the east, Reuben on the south, Ephraim on the west, and Dan on the north. The same order was followed when Israel broke camp and marched.

---

### v. 1 — "Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron…"

**Traditional Reading:** The command comes after the census of chapter 1 was completed. The Pulpit Commentary suggests this was given "probably when they had finished the census, and brought the results into the tabernacle" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html). Gill notes that the directions are given "when the congregation of Israel with the tabernacle were about to set forward on their journey; and therefore directions are here given for their orderly and regular proceeding" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html).

The inclusion of Aaron alongside Moses is significant: the order concerns not just military logistics but the arrangement of the people around God's dwelling, a matter that falls within priestly oversight as well as prophetic leadership.

---

### v. 2 — "The Israelites are to camp around the Tent of Meeting at a distance from it, each man under his standard, with the banners of his family."

**The phrase "at a distance" or "far off":** Ellicott argues that the Hebrew *minneged* is more accurately "over against" than "far off," meaning they faced the tabernacle with a space between, but the word does imply distance as well as opposition. He calculates the nearest tents were probably about 2,000 cubits (a Sabbath day's journey) from the tabernacle, yielding a camp area of about three square miles (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/2.htm). The Pulpit Commentary agrees: "over against, i.e., facing the tabernacle, with a certain space (perhaps 2000 cubits, Joshua 3:4) between" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html). Matthew Poole (cited by Enduring Word) says the distance was "partly out of reverence to God and his worship… and partly for caution, lest their vicinity to it might tempt them to make too near approaches to it" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-2/).

**"Standard" and "banners":** The Hebrew distinguishes between *degel* (the main standard or banner of the three-tribe group, sometimes also the tribe's own standard) and *othoth* (ensigns or signs for each father's house). The Pulpit Commentary: "Each tribe, it would seem, had its standard (*degel*), and each family in the tribe its ensign (*oth*)" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html). Ellicott similarly says, "Probably each father's house had its own smaller ensign or flag" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/2.htm). Gill says the ensigns were "lesser standards or banners… which were peculiar to their several families and houses, and distinguished one from another, like flags in different regiments" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html).

**Spiritual significance:** The Enduring Word commentary (David Guzik, broadly evangelical/charismatic) emphasizes that the command to organize was a major transition: "Israel had been on this Exodus journey for more than a year and had assembled in just about any way they had pleased. But now, ready to enter into the Promised Land, they had to take the next step in organization: Ordering themselves." Having been slaves (who do not organize themselves), they now had to learn the discipline of free people under God (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-2/). Dr. Constable's Expository Notes (from the search excerpts) note that "This arrangement placed Yahweh at the center of the nation geographically and reminded the Israelites that His rightful place was at the center of their life nationally and personally" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-2.html).

---

### v. 3 — "On the east side, toward the sunrise, the divisions of Judah are to camp under their standard…"

**East as the place of honour:** The Pulpit Commentary explains: "The van, the post of honour. The general direction indeed of their march was northwards, not eastwards; but nothing can obliterate the natural pre-eminence given to the east by the sunrise, the scattering of light upon the earth, the daily symbol of the day-spring from on high" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html). Enduring Word adds: "East is the place of the rising of the sun, the source of hope and sustenance. Westward was the sea. Israel's traditional stance was with its back to the ocean and the descent of the sun" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-2/).

**Why Judah first?** Not because of size (Dan's camp was larger than Reuben's and Ephraim's), but because of Judah's prophetic destiny. The Pulpit Commentary: "Judah led the way not because he was the greatest in number, for the order of the tribes was not determined by this consideration, but because of his place in prophecy, and as the ancestor of the Messiah (Genesis 49:10)" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html). Ellicott also notes: "It is quite possible that there may be a primary reference in Genesis 49:10 to the position which the camp of Judah should occupy in the marches of the Israelites" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/2.htm). The Expositor's Bible Commentary says simply: "The front is eastward, and Judah has the post of honour in the van" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/numbers-2.html).

---

### vv. 4–9 — The Camp of Judah (East Side)

**v. 4: Nahshon son of Amminadab** — He appears in the genealogy of David and Jesus (Ruth 4:20–22; Matthew 1:4). He is the prince of Judah, also listed in Numbers 1:7 and 7:12.

**v. 5: The tribe of Issachar camps next to Judah.** Gill notes the family logic: Issachar and Zebulun "were the brethren of Judah, by the same mother Leah, and so fitly put together, as most likely to continue in harmony and love; and being the youngest sons of Leah, and brethren of Judah, would, without any reluctance or murmuring, pitch under their elder brother's standard" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html).

**v. 9: "They shall set out first."** The camp of Judah numbered 186,400 men — the largest of the four camps. Gill observes: "this was the largest camp of them all, being near 30,000 more than Dan's… and therefore placed foremost, and as the vanguard to the tabernacle" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html). The Pulpit Commentary notes that no explicit command to set forth had yet been given in the narrative; "but the necessity of doing so was understood, and is here anticipated" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html).

---

### vv. 10–16 — The Camp of Reuben (South Side)

**The south side:** The Pulpit Commentary identifies this as the right wing, with the tribes of Reuben, Simeon, and Gad. Gill notes: "Reuben and Simeon being brothers by the mother as well as the father's side, might well be thought to agree together; and Reuben being the eldest brother, and the eldest of all Jacob's sons, Simeon would not grudge to pitch under him" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html).

**Gad under Reuben:** Gill notes Gad was "the eldest son of Leah's handmaid Zilpah, is fitly placed under Leah's firstborn" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html).

**v. 14: Eliasaph son of Deuel** — The Pulpit Commentary notes that "Reuel" in some manuscripts is "probably an error of transcription for Deuel," and adds: "The error is utterly unimportant, except as proving the possibility of errors in the sacred text" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html). Ellicott concurs: "There is good authority for reading Deuel here" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/2.htm). Gill notes the Hebrew letters *resh* and *daleth* are similar and sometimes interchanged (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html).

**v. 16: "They shall set out second."** The total is 151,450 men. Gill notes: "they in journeying moving next to the camp of Judah, and before the tabernacle; for though, while encamped, the camp of Reuben lay on the south, or right side of it, yet, when marching, went before it" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html).

---

### v. 17 — "In the middle of the camps, the Tent of Meeting is to travel with the camp of the Levites…"

**Central placement of the tabernacle:** This verse describes both the stationary encampment and the marching order. The Pulpit Commentary says: "Thus it was provided that, whether at rest or on the march, the Divine habitation should be exactly in the midst of Israel" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html). Ellicott makes a connection to the Psalms: "As the sanctuary of God was in the midst of the camp of the Israelites, and set forward in the midst of their hosts as they marched, so God is represented by the Psalmist as being in the midst of His Church (Psalm 46:5)" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/2.htm).

**Marching order of the Levites:** Gill, citing Aben Ezra, explains the practical order: "the Gershonites and Merarites marched between the standard of Judah and the standard of Reuben; and the Kohathites marched, and with them Aaron and his sons, between the standard of Reuben and the standard of Ephraim" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html). Thus the tabernacle components were carried in two groups, separated by the camp of Reuben, ensuring the most holy items (carried by the Kohathites) were in the safest central position.

**Family basis of the arrangement:** Ellicott observes that "the collocation of the tribes was evidently determined in accordance with their mutual relationship." The eastern camp was all Leah's sons; the southern camp was the remaining Leah sons plus Zilpah's son Gad; the western camp was Rachel's descendants; and the northern camp was the sons of the handmaids Bilhah and Zilpah. He notes that "if allowance be made for the separation of the tribe of Levi, none could have been made in which the relationship by birth would be more closely adhered to" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/2.htm). Ellicott further observes that in the later territorial allotments, the temporary wilderness groupings were largely preserved: Issachar and Zebulun had adjoining territories; Reuben and Gad were neighbours east of the Jordan; Benjamin, Manasseh, and Ephraim were together in the central hill country; and Asher and Naphtali were neighbours in the north (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/2.htm).

---

### vv. 18–24 — The Camp of Ephraim (West Side)

**v. 18: Ephraim on the west** — Though Manasseh was the elder son of Joseph, Ephraim is given the standard-bearing role, consistent with Jacob's blessing (Genesis 48:17–20). Gill: "though the elder brother to Ephraim, yet Ephraim was preferred to him, and had a standard given him, and his elder brother was directed to pitch by it; and this being agreeably to the prophecy of Jacob, could not well be objected to" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html).

**The Rachel tribes:** Ellicott notes these three tribes formed the smallest of the four camps at 108,100 men. The Pulpit Commentary observes: "All the descendants of Rachel, forming at this time the smallest of the four divisions, although destined to become very numerous. Their association in the camp was continued in the promised land, for the greater part of their territory was coterminous. Subsequently, however, the great division of the kingdom separated Benjamin for ever from his brethren" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html).

**v. 24: "They shall set out third"** — immediately behind the tabernacle. The Pulpit Commentary notes this position "is clearly alluded to in Psalm 80:1, 2" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html), where the psalmist calls on God who is enthroned "before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh."

---

### vv. 25–31 — The Camp of Dan (North Side)

**v. 25: Dan on the north** — Dan's camp numbered 157,600, the second largest. Gill notes the arrangement: "Dan had a standard given him, though the son of an handmaid, being the firstborn of the sons of the handmaids, and his tribe being a warlike tribe, and very numerous" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html).

**The Pulpit Commentary's reflection on Dan:** "In the light of its subsequent history, it is remarkable that this tribe should at this time have been so prominent and so honoured. Dan is, so to speak, the Judas among the twelve. In history he ends by melting away into the heathen among whom he intruded himself. In the sacred writings he ends by being omitted altogether; he has no part in the new Jerusalem — perhaps on account of the idolatry connected with his name (see Judges 18; Revelation 7)" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html).

**v. 31: "They shall set out last, under their standards."** Dan's camp formed the rear guard. Gill notes the strategic wisdom: "so that it had in its van and rear the two largest camps, which were wisely ordered for its safety" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html). Ellicott adds that "standards" here is a plural used for the singular, or may encompass the ensigns of the individual tribes within the camp (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/2.htm).

---

### vv. 32–34 — Summary and Conclusion

**v. 32: Total of 603,550** — This is the same total as Numbers 1:46. Gill marvels at the growth: "It is a large number, considering in how short a time, and that great part of it a state of bondage, from seventy persons, they rose unto it; but the spiritual Israel of God, consisting of his people of all nations, is a number which no man can number, Revelation 7:9" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html). Ellicott makes the same observation, contrasting this number with "the spiritual Israel of Revelation 7:9" which "is represented as a great multitude which no man could number" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/2.htm).

**v. 33: The Levites not counted** — This reiterates Numbers 1:47–49. The Levites were a separate camp, dedicated to the service of the tabernacle, exempt from military duty.

**v. 34: Israel's obedience** — The chapter ends by emphasizing that Israel did everything exactly as commanded. Enduring Word notes: "This verse also speaks of significant order — a major accomplishment for a people so numerous, so recently enslaved, and more recently a mob in disarray" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-2/).

---

## The Four Standards and the Living Creatures

One of the most discussed features of Numbers 2 across all traditions is the possible correspondence between the tribal standards and the four living creatures seen by Ezekiel (Ezekiel 1:10) and John (Revelation 4:7).

**The tradition:** Jewish sources (cited by multiple commentators) assign a lion to Judah (cf. Genesis 49:9), a man to Reuben (cf. the mandrakes of Genesis 30:14), an ox/calf to Ephraim (cf. Deuteronomy 33:17), and an eagle to Dan. The Pulpit Commentary cites Aben Ezra for this assignment and notes: "If it were so, we should find in these banners the origin of the forms of the living creatures in the visions of Ezekiel and St. John" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html). The Expositor's Bible Commentary concurs: "If this tradition is accepted, it will connect the four main ensigns of Israel with the vision of Ezekiel" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/numbers-2.html).

**Cautions expressed:** However, Enduring Word provides a detailed table showing how widely the traditions vary — with different Jewish sources giving completely different emblems (fish, stag, serpent, unicorn, olive tree, etc.). David Guzik concludes: "In summary, we don't have firm biblical evidence for what appeared on the standard" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-2/). The Pulpit Commentary similarly notes: "the tradition of the Jews is too fluctuating to carry any weight. The Targum of Palestine assigns to Judah the lion, but to Reuben a stag, to Ephraim a young man, and to Dan a basilisk serpent" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html). Enduring Word cites Keil and Delitzsch who "admit 'Neither the Mosaic law, nor the Old Testament generally, gives us any intimation as to the form or character of the standard'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-2/).

Nevertheless, even if unprovable historically, the typological connection is widely embraced as spiritually suggestive across evangelical and Reformed traditions.

---

## Points Where Traditions Differ

**1. Typological vs. Historical-Literal Reading:** Traditional evangelical, Reformed, and Baptist commentators (Gill, Matthew Henry, JFB) read the camp arrangement strongly typologically — as an emblem of the Church under Christ. Gill explicitly says: "Now this encampment of the people of Israel was an emblem of the form and order of the spiritual Israel or church of God, under the Gospel dispensation. Christ in human nature is the tabernacle, who is in the midst of his people by his gracious presence" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html). The Pulpit Commentary's homiletics develop this extensively (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html). More modern evangelical sources like Constable and Enduring Word tend to focus more on practical application (God is a God of order; God must be at the centre) and historical context, while still acknowledging typological dimensions.

**2. The "ideal" vs. "real" encampment:** The Pulpit Commentary notably suggests the arrangement may have been partly ideal rather than fully realized: "We must conclude, therefore, that this order of encampment was an ideal order, beautiful indeed by reason of its faultless regularity and equality, but only to be attained in practice as circumstances should permit, more or less." It argues that the foursquare symmetry "had an ideal meaning and significance more really, because more permanently, important than its actual realization at the time, is evident from its recurrence again and again in the Apocalyptic writings (see Ezekiel 48:20, and especially Revelation 21:16)" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-2.html). Other older commentaries (Gill, JFB, Ellicott) treat the arrangement as literal and actually practiced, with calculations of the square mileage required. The JFB commentary computes "somewhat more than twelve square miles" for the camp (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/numbers/2.htm).

**3. Pentecostal/Charismatic perspective:** The Enduring Word commentary (David Guzik, broadly charismatic) places strong emphasis on practical application for the believer's life — the need to be organized and disciplined as spiritual progress, the centrality of God's presence, and the idea that "nothing is accomplished in God's kingdom without order and organization" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-2/). There is less emphasis on ecclesiological typology and more on personal and corporate spiritual discipline.

**4. Baptist perspective (Gill):** Gill, writing as a Calvinistic Baptist, reads Numbers 2 through a strongly Christocentric and ecclesiologically typological lens. He sees Christ in the tabernacle, the ministers of the word in the Levites, and the whole church arranged around Christ. His exposition is characteristically thorough on textual and rabbinic details (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-2.html). The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary (from search excerpts) focuses on the practical arrangement, noting "No information is extant on the arrangement of the camp prior to the census" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-2.html).

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (Egyptian parallel):** Dr. Constable's Expository Notes cite B. Maarsingh: "The Egyptians characteristically placed the tent of the king, his generals, and officers at the center of a large army camp, but for the Israelites another tent was central: the sanctuary in which it placed God to dwell among his people" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-2.html). Enduring Word similarly cites Wenham: "The Egyptian army under Rameses II (13th century B.C.) adopted this formation in camp. They camped in a square with the royal tent in the middle. Likewise Israel's king dwelt in the centre of his armies in the tent of meeting" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-2/). This parallel suggests Israel's camp was deliberately modelled on Egyptian military practice but with God rather than Pharaoh at the centre — a polemical statement about who is the true King.

**Catholic/Orthodox readings:** No specific Catholic or Orthodox pages on Numbers 2 were retrieved in the search results. However, the typological reading common in the older Protestant commentaries (the camp as the Church, the tabernacle as Christ or the Eucharist, the foursquare shape as the heavenly Jerusalem) is broadly shared with Catholic and Orthodox interpretive traditions, which also read the Old Testament camp and tabernacle as figures of the Church and the heavenly liturgy.

**Debated popular teaching:** No specific prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace readings of Numbers 2 were found in the search results. Numbers 2 is not a text typically disputed along these lines.

---

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

| Theme | Source |
|---|---|
| God must be at the centre of His people's life and order | All sources |
| The camp as emblem of the Church under Christ | Gill, Pulpit, Ellicott, Expositor's |
| The four standards possibly corresponding to Revelation's living creatures | Pulpit, Expositor's, Enduring Word, Gill |
| The east as the place of honour and hope | Pulpit, Enduring Word, Constable |
| Judah's primacy based on Messianic prophecy, not size | Pulpit, Ellicott |
| Family relationships determining tribal groupings | Ellicott, Gill |
| God is a God of order, not confusion | Enduring Word, Pulpit, Constable |
| The arrangement may have been partly ideal | Pulpit Commentary |
| Egyptian military camp as the cultural model, subverted | Constable, Enduring Word (citing Wenham) |
